claims.text: The alloy under study is equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous bulk composition and a pristine surface without pre-formed oxides.
Oxidation resistance and material integrity are governed by the evolution of the surface oxide.
Oxidation proceeds through an initial selective-oxidation stage followed by a diffusion-controlled oxide-growth stage.
Element-specific redox-potential differences drive selective oxidation during the initial stage.
Initial selective oxidation produces a uniform, adherent, protective oxide layer.
Species transport through the alloy, oxide-metal interface, and oxide layer contributes to oxide-scale growth.
Atomic-size differences become dominant at later times and cause compositional inversion.
Compositional inversion and diffusion limitations subsequently control oxide thickening or degradation.
Lower oxygen partial pressures favor selective oxidation and formation of a uniform, adherent oxide.
Higher oxygen partial pressures cause rapid initial oxidation followed by accelerated atomic diffusion.
At high oxygen partial pressure, atomic-size differences cause compositional inversion, nonuniform scale thickening, and loss of oxide-layer integrity.
Relative to moderate oxygen partial pressure, lower oxygen partial pressure delays rapid oxide thickening.
Relative to moderate oxygen partial pressure, higher oxygen partial pressure produces an earlier transition to a diffusion-limited regime and a thicker, potentially less-adherent scale.
A distinct transition point should separate the selective-oxidation and diffusion-controlled regimes.
Oxidation near 20% O2 at high temperature provides a baseline oxide-scale growth profile for CoCrFeNiMn.
The mechanism should hold for equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn from 900 to 1200 °C over the tested oxygen partial pressures.
In-situ atom-probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy can resolve oxidation-induced compositional and structural evolution.
Failure to observe either a regime transition or reproducible oxygen-pressure-dependent shifts in kinetics and morphology would falsify the proposed mechanism.
